nameStory: One look at this mushroom and you'll understand its name perfectly – it really does look like a lion's shaggy mane! The long, white, dangling spines cascade downward just like the flowing hair of the king of beasts. In Japan, it's called yamabushitake, named after the long white hair of mountain hermit monks.
description: Lion's mane is one of the most distinctive mushrooms you'll ever see – it looks nothing like the typical cap-and-stem mushrooms most people know. Instead, it forms a large, white, shaggy mass that hangs from tree trunks like a fluffy pom-pom. The entire mushroom is covered in long, soft spines that dangle downward, giving it an unmistakable appearance. It can grow quite large, sometimes reaching the size of a softball or even bigger.

idTips.label: Spines
idTips.description: Long white spines hang downward like icicles, each longer than half an inch. They're soft to touch and will bend easily when you brush them with your finger.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms a single, compact clump rather than branching like coral. The whole mushroom looks like one big white puff ball with dangling fringe.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pure white when fresh, aging to cream or slightly yellowish. Older specimens may develop brown or pinkish tinges at the tips of the spines.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels spongy and soft when pressed gently. The spines are tender and will compress easily under light pressure, springing back when released.

idTips.label: Attachment
idTips.description: Grows directly from tree trunks or large branches without a visible stem. It appears to emerge right out of the bark, often from wounds or dead spots.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Fresh specimens have a pleasant, mild mushroom scent – earthy but not strong. Some people detect a slightly seafood-like aroma, often compared to crab or lobster.

habitat: Lion's mane grows exclusively on hardwood trees, especially American beech and maple trees throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests. You'll find it on both dead trees and living trees with wounds, typically on the main trunk or large branches rather than small twigs. It prefers mature forest settings from sea level up into the mountains.

seasonality.spring: No fruiting bodies present. The mushroom's thread-like mycelium is quietly growing inside dead wood, invisible to casual observers.
seasonality.summer: Early fruiting may begin in late summer, especially after periods of warm, humid weather. Look for small, developing white masses on tree trunks.
seasonality.fall: Prime season for lion's mane! Late summer through autumn brings the best fruiting, with large, mature specimens appearing after rain. This is when you're most likely to spot these distinctive white pom-poms.
seasonality.winter: Fruiting bodies die back with hard frosts. Dried, brown remnants may still cling to trees, but fresh mushrooms won't appear until the following growing season.

funFact: Lion's mane mushrooms contain compounds that may support brain health, earning them the nickname 'smart mushrooms' – they're one of the few foods that might actually help your neurons grow new connections!
confusionNotes: Lion's mane is most easily confused with its close relatives bear's head tooth and coral tooth fungus, but those species have branching structures that look more like coral or cauliflower. Remember: if it's one big fluffy ball with straight-hanging spines, it's lion's mane – if it branches like coral, it's one of the other tooth fungi.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'tooth fungus,' lion's mane doesn't have teeth at all – the 'teeth' are actually the long spines that hang down. This whole group gets its name because many species in the family have short, pointed projections that do look more like actual teeth.
compareHints: Lion's mane stands out from its Hericium relatives by forming a single, unbranched mass – think of a white pom-pom hanging from a tree. Bear's head tooth and coral tooth fungus both have multiple branches that divide and subdivide like coral or cauliflower. Lion's mane also typically grows larger than its branching cousins and has the longest spines in the group.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Hericium relatives, Bear's Head Tooth has the most pronounced branching structure with the longest dangling teeth.

Coral tooth fungus is much more intricately branched than its Hericium relatives - while lion's mane looks like a white waterfall of long spines and bear's head forms compact clusters, coral tooth creates the most complex branching pattern with shorter spines.
